claim: Botryllus schlosseri is a colonial urochordate that follows the chordate plan of development following sexual reproduction.
source: Botryllus schlosseri is a colonial urochordate that follows the chordate plan of development following sexual reproduction, but invokes a stem cell-mediated budding program during subsequent rounds of asexual reproduction.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the organism's developmental characteristics.

claim: Botryllus schlosseri invokes a stem cell-mediated budding program during asexual reproduction.
source: Botryllus schlosseri is a colonial urochordate that follows the chordate plan of development following sexual reproduction, but invokes a stem cell-mediated budding program during subsequent rounds of asexual reproduction.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the organism's asexual reproduction mechanism.

claim: Urochordates are considered to be the closest living invertebrate relatives of vertebrates.
source: As urochordates are considered to be the closest living invertebrate relatives of vertebrates, they are ideal subjects for whole genome sequence analyses.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific consensus and is cited elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: The B. schlosseri genome assembly is 580 Mbp.
source: Using a novel method for high-throughput sequencing of eukaryotic genomes, we sequenced and assembled 580 Mbp of the B. schlosseri genome.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported from the sequencing and assembly work performed in this study.

claim: The B. schlosseri genome contains nearly 14,000 intron-containing predicted genes.
source: The genome assembly is comprised of nearly 14,000 intron-containing predicted genes, and 13,500 intron-less predicted genes, 40% of which could be confidently parceled into 13 (of 16 haploid) chromosomes.
evidence: This is a direct result from the gene prediction analysis performed on the assembled genome.

claim: The B. schlosseri genome contains 13,500 intron-less predicted genes.
source: The genome assembly is comprised of nearly 14,000 intron-containing predicted genes, and 13,500 intron-less predicted genes, 40% of which could be confidently parceled into 13 (of 16 haploid) chromosomes.
evidence: This is a direct result from the gene prediction analysis performed on the assembled genome.

claim: 40% of B. schlosseri predicted genes could be confidently parceled into 13 chromosomes.
source: The genome assembly is comprised of nearly 14,000 intron-containing predicted genes, and 13,500 intron-less predicted genes, 40% of which could be confidently parceled into 13 (of 16 haploid) chromosomes.
evidence: This is a direct result from the chromosome assignment analysis performed in this study.

claim: B. schlosseri has 16 haploid chromosomes.
source: The genome assembly is comprised of nearly 14,000 intron-containing predicted genes, and 13,500 intron-less predicted genes, 40% of which could be confidently parceled into 13 (of 16 haploid) chromosomes.
evidence: This is based on previous cytological studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: In 1866, Russian embryologist Alexander Kowalevsky wrote to Charles Darwin about the extensive developmental and morphological similarities between ascidian larvae and vertebrates.
source: In 1866, Russian embryologist Alexander Kowalevsky wrote to Charles Darwin about the extensive developmental and morphological similarities between ascidian larvae and vertebrates, leading Darwin to hypothesize that ascidians (belonging to urochordates or tunicates) might be crucial to understanding the origin of the vertebrate phylum (Darwin, 1874).
evidence: This is a historical fact cited with a reference to Darwin's work.

claim: Darwin hypothesized that ascidians might be crucial to understanding the origin of the vertebrate phylum.
source: In 1866, Russian embryologist Alexander Kowalevsky wrote to Charles Darwin about the extensive developmental and morphological similarities between ascidian larvae and vertebrates, leading Darwin to hypothesize that ascidians (belonging to urochordates or tunicates) might be crucial to understanding the origin of the vertebrate phylum (Darwin, 1874).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citation to Darwin's 1874 work.

claim: Tunicates are the closest extant relatives of vertebrates.
source: Indeed, tunicates are the closest extant relatives of vertebrates (Delsuc et al., 2006), and represent an investigative model for evolutionary events leading to adaptive immunity (Sabbadin, 1962; Scofield et al., 1982) and vertebrate-specific organ/tissue complexity (Dehal et al., 2002; Jeffery et al., 2004; Abitua et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Delsuc et al., 2006.

claim: Tunicates represent an investigative model for evolutionary events leading to adaptive immunity.
source: Indeed, tunicates are the closest extant relatives of vertebrates (Delsuc et al., 2006), and represent an investigative model for evolutionary events leading to adaptive immunity (Sabbadin, 1962; Scofield et al., 1982) and vertebrate-specific organ/tissue complexity (Dehal et al., 2002; Jeffery et al., 2004; Abitua et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sabbadin, 1962 and Scofield et al., 1982.

claim: Tunicates represent an investigative model for vertebrate-specific organ/tissue complexity.
source: Indeed, tunicates are the closest extant relatives of vertebrates (Delsuc et al., 2006), and represent an investigative model for evolutionary events leading to adaptive immunity (Sabbadin, 1962; Scofield et al., 1982) and vertebrate-specific organ/tissue complexity (Dehal et al., 2002; Jeffery et al., 2004; Abitua et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dehal et al., 2002; Jeffery et al., 2004; Abitua et al., 2012.

claim: Botryllus schlosseri is an invasive colonial urochordate living in large communities.
source: Botryllus schlosseri is an invasive colonial urochordate, living in large communities consisting of multiple colonies organized into expansive mats that coat a variety of marine surfaces, such as rocks, molluscs, multicellular algae, and ship hulls (Stoner et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the organism's ecology, supported by citation.

claim: B. schlosseri colonies coat a variety of marine surfaces including rocks, molluscs, multicellular algae, and ship hulls.
source: Botryllus schlosseri is an invasive colonial urochordate, living in large communities consisting of multiple colonies organized into expansive mats that coat a variety of marine surfaces, such as rocks, molluscs, multicellular algae, and ship hulls (Stoner et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the organism's habitat, supported by citation.

claim: B. schlosseri communities develop among compatible colonies governed by a genetically encoded histocompatibility system.
source: Communities develop among compatible colonies, governed by a genetically encoded histocompatibility system (Sabbadin, 1962; Scofield et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sabbadin, 1962 and Scofield et al., 1982.

claim: The progeny of each B. schlosseri colony usually represents a clone of vascularly connected, asexually reproducing individuals derived from a single planktonic larva.
source: The progeny of each colony usually represents a clone of the vascularly connected, asexually reproducing individuals (zooids) derived from a single planktonic larva (Manni and Burighel, 2006; Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manni and Burighel, 2006 and reference to Figure 1A-D.

claim: Compatible B. schlosseri colonies fuse their blood vessels to generate a chimera.
source: Compatible colonies fuse their blood vessels to generate a chimera, while incompatible colonies reject one another, maintaining individuality (Sabbadin, 1962; Scofield et al., 1982; Voskoboynik et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sabbadin, 1962; Scofield et al., 1982; Voskoboynik et al., 2013.

claim: Incompatible B. schlosseri colonies reject one another, maintaining individuality.
source: Compatible colonies fuse their blood vessels to generate a chimera, while incompatible colonies reject one another, maintaining individuality (Sabbadin, 1962; Scofield et al., 1982; Voskoboynik et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sabbadin, 1962; Scofield et al., 1982; Voskoboynik et al., 2013.

claim: Following fusion of blood vessels between B. schlosseri colonies, circulating stem cells of one partner can compete and replace the germline and/or soma of the other partner.
source: Following the fusion of blood vessels between colonies, the circulating stem cells of one partner colony can compete and replace the germline and/or the soma of the other partner (Stoner and Weissman, 1996; Stoner et al., 1999; Laird et al., 2005; Voskoboynik et al., 2008; Rinkevich et al., 2013), a phenomenon analogous to allogeneic transplantation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The phenomenon of stem cell replacement in B. schlosseri chimeras is analogous to allogeneic transplantation.
source: Following the fusion of blood vessels between colonies, the circulating stem cells of one partner colony can compete and replace the germline and/or the soma of the other partner (Stoner and Weissman, 1996; Stoner et al., 1999; Laird et al., 2005; Voskoboynik et al., 2008; Rinkevich et al., 2013), a phenomenon analogous to allogeneic transplantation.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement comparing the biological phenomenon to a medical procedure.

claim: The B. schlosseri genome was previously estimated to be 725 Mb based on flow cytometry analysis.
source: The B. schlosseri genome was previously estimated to be 725 Mb based on flow cytometry analysis (De Tomaso et al., 1998), and metaphase spreads suggested that it is organized into 16 chromosomes (Colombera, 1963).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study that estimated genome size.

claim: Metaphase spreads suggested that the B. schlosseri genome is organized into 16 chromosomes.
source: The B. schlosseri genome was previously estimated to be 725 Mb based on flow cytometry analysis (De Tomaso et al., 1998), and metaphase spreads suggested that it is organized into 16 chromosomes (Colombera, 1963).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous cytological study.

claim: The LRseq approach increases the read length of a next generation sequencer by 50-fold.
source: This long read sequencing approach (LRseq) effectively increases the read length of a next generation sequencer by 50-fold, while decreasing the error rate by orders of magnitude (Figure 2; 'Materials and methods' under 'Genome sequencing and assembly').
evidence: This is a claim about the technical performance of the LRseq method developed in this study, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The LRseq approach decreases the error rate by orders of magnitude.
source: This long read sequencing approach (LRseq) effectively increases the read length of a next generation sequencer by 50-fold, while decreasing the error rate by orders of magnitude (Figure 2; 'Materials and methods' under 'Genome sequencing and assembly').
evidence: This is a claim about the technical performance of the LRseq method developed in this study, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The LRseq approach began with genomic DNA sheared to 6-8 kb fragments.
source: Our approach began with genomic DNA sheared to 6–8 kb fragments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used in this study.

claim: Limiting dilution was used to create aliquots of a few hundred to a few thousand DNA molecules in the LRseq approach.
source: Limiting dilution was used to create aliquots of a few hundred to a few thousand DNA molecules.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used in this study.

claim: Each aliquot in LRseq was amplified with PCR, fragmented (600-800 bp), barcoded, and sequenced by Illumina HiSeq 2000.
source: Each aliquot was amplified with PCR, fragmented (600–800 bp), barcoded, and sequenced by Illumina HiSeq 2000 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used in this study, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The Velvet assembler was used to assemble short paired-end reads from each barcode separately in the LRseq approach.
source: The Velvet assembler (Zerbino, 2010) was used to assemble short paired-end reads from each barcode (i.e., well) separately, thus simplifying the assembly problem and creating effective read lengths corresponding to the original large fragment sizes (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 2A, Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the computational method used in this study.

claim: Limiting the number of DNA molecules per well greatly reduces or eliminates chances of having a repeated or duplicate sequence within a defined partition.
source: Limiting the number of DNA molecules per well greatly reduces or eliminates chances of having a repeated or duplicate sequence within a defined partition.
evidence: This is a logical explanation of how the LRseq method addresses repetitive sequences.

claim: Over-sequencing each well reduces the error rate by the coverage and substantially improves from the intrinsic error rate of the sequencer.
source: Furthermore, since each well was over-sequenced, the error rate is reduced by the coverage and is substantially improved from the intrinsic error rate of the sequencer (Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: This is an explanation of how the LRseq method improves sequencing accuracy, supported by data in Supplementary file 2C.

claim: Data from twelve 96-well plates were obtained using the LRseq procedure.
source: This procedure is amenable to automation in multiwell plates, and we obtained data from twelve 96-well plates (Supplementary file 2A, Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the scale of the experimental work performed.

claim: The LRseq method was validated on human genomic DNA.
source: We validated this method on human genomic DNA, for which an independent reference is available (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of validation experiments performed, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The conventional sequencing and assembly from colony Sc6a-b DNA achieved an average N50 of 1 kb.
source: This Sc6a-b assembly achieved an average N50 of 1 kb, yielding short contigs that were insufficient for whole genome assembly (Supplementary file 2D).
evidence: This is a result from the conventional sequencing approach, reported in Supplementary file 2D.

claim: LRseq applied to the 356a clone obtained a 566 Mbp assembly with an N50 of 7kb.
source: By contrast, when we applied LRseq to the 356a clone, we obtained a 566 Mbp assembly with a dramatically improved N50 of 7kb (Supplementary file 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from the LRseq approach, reported in Supplementary file 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The LRseq approach simplified the assembly of a complex eukaryotic genome.
source: This approach not only simplified the assembly of a complex eukaryotic genome, but also reduced the confounding impact of repetitive DNA on contig assembly (Figure 2C–D; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the benefits of the LRseq method, supported by data in figures.

claim: The LRseq approach reduced the confounding impact of repetitive DNA on contig assembly.
source: This approach not only simplified the assembly of a complex eukaryotic genome, but also reduced the confounding impact of repetitive DNA on contig assembly (Figure 2C–D; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the benefits of the LRseq method, supported by data in figures.

claim: Using 21 chromosome mixtures, 356a genomic contigs larger than 7 kb were aligned to chromosome reads using BWA.
source: Using the 21 chromosome mixtures, containing between 1 and 4 chromosomes each, 356a genomic contigs larger than 7 kb were aligned to the chromosome reads using BWA.
evidence: This is a description of the computational method used for chromosome assignment.

claim: Scaffolds were assigned to chromosome clusters by iterative K-means clustering on the correlation matrix between each scaffold.
source: Then, scaffolds were assigned to chromosome clusters by iterative K-means clustering on the correlation matrix between each scaffold (Figure 3; 'Materials and methods' under 'Chromosome sequencing, assignment and assembly').
evidence: This is a description of the computational method used for chromosome assignment, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: The chromosome assignment approach clearly resolves 13 chromosomes with a mean chromosome meta-scaffold size of 16,234 kb and a mean N50 of 38 kb.
source: Assuming that B. schlosseri carries 16x2 chromosomes (Colombera, 1963), this approach clearly resolves 13 chromosomes with a mean chromosome meta-scaffold size of 16,234 kb and a mean N50 of 38 kb (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2D).
evidence: This is a result from the chromosome assignment analysis, reported in figures and supplementary files.

claim: The final B. schlosseri draft assembly is 580 Mbp with an improved N50.
source: An overall improvement in N50 was achieved, yielding a final 580 Mbp draft assembly (Supplementary file 2D).
evidence: This is the final result of the genome assembly work, reported in Supplementary file 2D.

claim: 6601 interspersed repeat families were identified in the B. schlosseri genome, each present in at least three copies.
source: We identified 6601 interspersed repeat families, each present in at least three copies, that together cover ∼65% of the B. schlosseri genome assembly (Supplementary file 2E).
evidence: This is a result from the repeat analysis performed on the genome assembly.

claim: Interspersed repeat families cover approximately 65% of the B. schlosseri genome assembly.
source: We identified 6601 interspersed repeat families, each present in at least three copies, that together cover ∼65% of the B. schlosseri genome assembly (Supplementary file 2E).
evidence: This is a result from the repeat analysis performed on the genome assembly.

claim: 1400 large repeat families (interspersed repeats with genomic alignments of at least 1 kb) were identified in B. schlosseri.
source: We also identified 1400 large repeat families, defined as interspersed repeats with genomic alignments of at least 1 kb.
evidence: This is a result from the repeat analysis performed on the genome assembly.

claim: Large interspersed repeats in B. schlosseri are found in a median of four chromosomes.
source: Notably, large interspersed repeats are found in a median of four chromosomes (of 13 chromosome assignments), and >10% of large interspersed repeat families occur in over 100 copies (Supplementary file 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the repeat analysis, reported in supplementary files and figures.

claim: More than 10% of large interspersed repeat families in B. schlosseri occur in over 100 copies.
source: Notably, large interspersed repeats are found in a median of four chromosomes (of 13 chromosome assignments), and >10% of large interspersed repeat families occur in over 100 copies (Supplementary file 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the repeat analysis, reported in supplementary files and figures.

claim: Approximately 3.2 million tandem repeats were identified in the B. schlosseri genome, with periods ranging from 1-6525 bp and copy numbers ranging from 2-1096x.
source: In all, ∼3.2 million tandem repeats were identified, with periods ranging from 1–6525 bp and copy numbers ranging from 2–1096x (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the tandem repeat analysis using XSTREAM, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The human genome contains over 50% repeats.
source: By comparison, the human genome was assembled to a very high standard using conventional Sanger technology and later Illumina technology, and was found to contain over 50% repeats (de Konning et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparative statement citing a previous study on the human genome.

claim: All B. schlosseri genes (n = 66) available from NCBI aligned with the B. schlosseri draft assembly.
source: All B. schlosseri genes (n = 66), fosmid sequences (n = 11) and most of the 98,611 expressed sequence tags (ESTs) available from NCBI aligned with the B. schlosseri draft assembly (Supplementary file 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 5; 'Materials and methods' under 'Evaluation of 365a-chromosomes hybrid assembly').
evidence: This is a validation result showing concordance between the assembly and independent sequence data.

claim: All fosmid sequences (n = 11) available from NCBI aligned with the B. schlosseri draft assembly.
source: All B. schlosseri genes (n = 66), fosmid sequences (n = 11) and most of the 98,611 expressed sequence tags (ESTs) available from NCBI aligned with the B. schlosseri draft assembly (Supplementary file 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 5; 'Materials and methods' under 'Evaluation of 365a-chromosomes hybrid assembly').
evidence: This is a validation result showing concordance between the assembly and independent sequence data.

claim: Most of the 98,611 expressed sequence tags (ESTs) available from NCBI aligned with the B. schlosseri draft assembly.
source: All B. schlosseri genes (n = 66), fosmid sequences (n = 11) and most of the 98,611 expressed sequence tags (ESTs) available from NCBI aligned with the B. schlosseri draft assembly (Supplementary file 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 5; 'Materials and methods' under 'Evaluation of 365a-chromosomes hybrid assembly').
evidence: This is a validation result showing concordance between the assembly and independent sequence data.

claim: Nearly all (93%) of the independently sequenced and assembled Roche 454 Sc6a-b contigs were successfully mapped to the assembly.
source: Moreover, nearly all of the independently sequenced and assembled Roche 454 Sc6a-b contigs (93%) were successfully mapped to the assembly (Supplementary files 2F; 'Materials and methods' under 'Evaluation of 365a-chromosomes hybrid assembly').
evidence: This is a validation result showing concordance between the assembly and independent sequence data.

claim: 38,730 putative protein-coding loci were identified in the B. schlosseri genome, all with at least 30% transcript support.
source: In total, 38,730 putative protein-coding loci were identified, all of which have at least 30% transcript support ('Materials and methods' under 'RNA sequencing', 'Gene prediction', 'Gene annotation'; Supplementary file 2I).
evidence: This is a result from the gene prediction analysis performed on the genome assembly.

claim: Among the predicted B. schlosseri genes, 27,463 include a start and stop codon.
source: Among these predicted genes, 27,463 include a start and stop codon, 13,910 genes have at least one intron, and 13,553 are intron-less (Supplementary file 2H).
evidence: This is a result from the gene prediction analysis.

claim: 13,910 B. schlosseri genes have at least one intron.
source: Among these predicted genes, 27,463 include a start and stop codon, 13,910 genes have at least one intron, and 13,553 are intron-less (Supplementary file 2H).
evidence: This is a result from the gene prediction analysis.

claim: 13,553 B. schlosseri genes are intron-less.
source: Among these predicted genes, 27,463 include a start and stop codon, 13,910 genes have at least one intron, and 13,553 are intron-less (Supplementary file 2H).
evidence: This is a result from the gene prediction analysis.

claim: For each B. schlosseri chromosome, 55% of genes have at least one intron while approximately 45% are intron-less.
source: Moreover, for each of the B. schlosseri chromosomes 55% of genes have at least one intron while ∼45% are intron-less (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a result from the gene structure analysis, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The mean B. schlosseri gene length is predicted to be 3.6 kbp.
source: In addition, the mean B. schlosseri gene length is predicted to be 3.6 kbp with a mean exon length of 170 bp (Supplementary file 2H).
evidence: This is a result from the gene structure analysis.

claim: The mean B. schlosseri exon length is 170 bp.
source: In addition, the mean B. schlosseri gene length is predicted to be 3.6 kbp with a mean exon length of 170 bp (Supplementary file 2H).
evidence: This is a result from the gene structure analysis.

claim: 144 out of 145 tested B. schlosseri genes (99.3%) were confirmed by PCR and Sanger-sequencing.
source: We tested a set of 145 genes by PCR and Sanger-sequencing, and were able to confirm 144 of them (99.3%), further validating the genome assembly (Figure 2—figure supplement 6, 'Materials and methods' under 'Evaluation of genes').
evidence: This is a validation result from experimental testing of predicted genes.

claim: Phylogenomic analysis of 425 conserved homologous genes across 15 diverse species supports the phylogenic position of tunicates within Chordata.
source: Phylogenomic analysis of 425 conserved homologous genes across 15 diverse species, and mitogenomic analysis of 65 species both support the phylogenic position of tunicates within Chordata (Delsuc et al., 2006; Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1; 'Materials and methods' under 'Mitochondrial phylogeny', 'Phylogenomic analyses'), and provide strong evidence that colonial and solitary tunicates represent the closest living relative of vertebrates.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis performed in this study, shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mitogenomic analysis of 65 species supports the phylogenic position of tunicates within Chordata.
source: Phylogenomic analysis of 425 conserved homologous genes across 15 diverse species, and mitogenomic analysis of 65 species both support the phylogenic position of tunicates within Chordata (Delsuc et al., 2006; Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1; 'Materials and methods' under 'Mitochondrial phylogeny', 'Phylogenomic analyses'), and provide strong evidence that colonial and solitary tunicates represent the closest living relative of vertebrates.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis performed in this study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Colonial and solitary tunicates represent the closest living relative of vertebrates.
source: Phylogenomic analysis of 425 conserved homologous genes across 15 diverse species, and mitogenomic analysis of 65 species both support the phylogenic position of tunicates within Chordata (Delsuc et al., 2006; Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1; 'Materials and methods' under 'Mitochondrial phylogeny', 'Phylogenomic analyses'), and provide strong evidence that colonial and solitary tunicates represent the closest living relative of vertebrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis performed in this study.

claim: 77% of human genes could be traced back to protochordates with at least some homology (e-value ≤ e−10).
source: Among the analyzed species, we found that 77% of human genes could be traced back to protochordates with at least some homology (e-value ≤ e−10), around 10% less than chicken (85%) and frog (86%) genomes, indicating that the common ancestral genome of tunicates and vertebrates had homology to at least 77% of the human gene repertoire.
evidence: This is a result from comparative genomic analysis performed in this study.

claim: 85% of human genes could be traced back to chicken with at least some homology.
source: Among the analyzed species, we found that 77% of human genes could be traced back to protochordates with at least some homology (e-value ≤ e−10), around 10% less than chicken (85%) and frog (86%) genomes, indicating that the common ancestral genome of tunicates and vertebrates had homology to at least 77% of the human gene repertoire.
evidence: This is a result from comparative genomic analysis performed in this study.

claim: 86% of human genes could be traced back to frog with at least some homology.
source: Among the analyzed species, we found that 77% of human genes could be traced back to protochordates with at least some homology (e-value ≤ e−10), around 10% less than chicken (85%) and frog (86%) genomes, indicating that the common ancestral genome of tunicates and vertebrates had homology to at least 77% of the human gene repertoire.
evidence: This is a result from comparative genomic analysis performed in this study.

claim: The common ancestral genome of tunicates and vertebrates had homology to at least 77% of the human gene repertoire.
source: Among the analyzed species, we found that 77% of human genes could be traced back to protochordates with at least some homology (e-value ≤ e−10), around 10% less than chicken (85%) and frog (86%) genomes, indicating that the common ancestral genome of tunicates and vertebrates had homology to at least 77% of the human gene repertoire.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparative genomic analysis.

claim: About 660 genes present in the common ancestor of tunicates and vertebrates are absent in non-chordate species.
source: This list includes about 660 genes present in the common ancestor, but absent in non-chordate species (Figure 4—source data 1B).
evidence: This is a result from comparative genomic analysis, reported in Figure 4—source data 1B.

claim: B. schlosseri has genes critical to the development and function of the vertebrate heart, including ALPK3 and TNNT2.
source: Among the genes found in B. schlosseri (either alone or in combination with other protochordate species) and vertebrates (Figure 4—source data 1B, Figure 4—source data 1C), we found genes that are critical to the development and function of the vertebrate heart (e.g., ALPK3, TNNT2; Hosoda et al., 2001; Frey et al., 2012), and eye (gamma and beta crystallins; Sun et al., 2011), and the ability to hear (GJB2/3/6 CLDN; Rabionet et al., 2000; Wilcox et al., 2001; Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1C).
evidence: This is a result from comparative genomic analysis, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: B. schlosseri has genes critical to the development and function of the vertebrate eye, including gamma and beta crystallins.
source: Among the genes found in B. schlosseri (either alone or in combination with other protochordate species) and vertebrates (Figure 4—source data 1B, Figure 4—source data 1C), we found genes that are critical to the development and function of the vertebrate heart (e.g., ALPK3, TNNT2; Hosoda et al., 2001; Frey et al., 2012), and eye (gamma and beta crystallins; Sun et al., 2011), and the ability to hear (GJB2/3/6 CLDN; Rabionet et al., 2000; Wilcox et al., 2001; Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1C).
evidence: This is a result from comparative genomic analysis, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: B. schlosseri has genes critical to the ability to hear, including GJB2/3/6 CLDN.
source: Among the genes found in B. schlosseri (either alone or in combination with other protochordate species) and vertebrates (Figure 4—source data 1B, Figure 4—source data 1C), we found genes that are critical to the development and function of the vertebrate heart (e.g., ALPK3, TNNT2; Hosoda et al., 2001; Frey et al., 2012), and eye (gamma and beta crystallins; Sun et al., 2011), and the ability to hear (GJB2/3/6 CLDN; Rabionet et al., 2000; Wilcox et al., 2001; Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1C).
evidence: This is a result from comparative genomic analysis, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations in ALPK3 and TNNT2 are implicated in heart diseases.
source: Mutations in these genes are implicated in a variety of human diseases and disorders, including heart diseases (Frey et al., 2012), cataracts (Sun et al., 2011), deafness (Rabionet et al., 2000; Wilcox et al., 2001), and nemaline myopathy (Johnston et al., 2000; Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Frey et al., 2012.

claim: Mutations in crystallin genes are implicated in cataracts.
source: Mutations in these genes are implicated in a variety of human diseases and disorders, including heart diseases (Frey et al., 2012), cataracts (Sun et al., 2011), deafness (Rabionet et al., 2000; Wilcox et al., 2001), and nemaline myopathy (Johnston et al., 2000; Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations in GJB2/3/6 CLDN genes are implicated in deafness.
source: Mutations in these genes are implicated in a variety of human diseases and disorders, including heart diseases (Frey et al., 2012), cataracts (Sun et al., 2011), deafness (Rabionet et al., 2000; Wilcox et al., 2001), and nemaline myopathy (Johnston et al., 2000; Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rabionet et al., 2000 and Wilcox et al., 2001.

claim: B. schlosseri was the only protochordate in the analysis with proteins homologous to pregnancy-specific glycoproteins (PSGs).
source: In addition, B. schlosseri was the only protochordate in our analysis with proteins homologous to pregnancy-specific glycoproteins (PSGs).
evidence: This is a result from comparative genomic analysis performed in this study.

claim: PSGs are the major placental polypeptides.
source: PSGs are the major placental polypeptides, and complications in pregnancies and spontaneous abortions have been associated with abnormally low levels of PSGs in the maternal blood (Camolotto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Camolotto et al., 2010.

claim: Complications in pregnancies and spontaneous abortions have been associated with abnormally low levels of PSGs in maternal blood.
source: PSGs are the major placental polypeptides, and complications in pregnancies and spontaneous abortions have been associated with abnormally low levels of PSGs in the maternal blood (Camolotto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Camolotto et al., 2010.

claim: A common blood supply among kin is established and tolerated in B. schlosseri chimeras, analogous to mammalian pregnancies.
source: Analogous to mammalian pregnancies, a common blood supply among kin is established and tolerated in B. schlosseri chimeras (Voskoboynik et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Voskoboynik et al., 2009 and represents an analogy drawn by the authors.

claim: Six genes unique to B. schlosseri and vertebrates (ZBTB1, MEFV, DSG3, NQO1, NQO2 and BHLHE40) are associated with increased leukocyte and hematopoietic cell numbers.
source: Six genes unique to B. schlosseri and vertebrates (ZBTB1, MEFV, DSG3, NQO1, NQO2 and BHLHE40) are associated with increased leukocyte and hematopoietic cell numbers (Figure 4—source data 1C; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a result from comparative genomic analysis, supported by citation to Chen et al., 2009.

claim: The six hematopoietic-related genes (ZBTB1, MEFV, DSG3, NQO1, NQO2 and BHLHE40) are absent in cephalochordates and solitary urochordates.
source: In our analysis, these genes are absent in cephalochordates and solitary urochordates, which all lack a defined vascular system (Moller and Philpott, 2005; Lemaire, 2011).
evidence: This is a result from comparative genomic analysis, with citations supporting the lack of vascular systems in these organisms.

claim: Cephalochordates and solitary urochordates lack a defined vascular system.
source: In our analysis, these genes are absent in cephalochordates and solitary urochordates, which all lack a defined vascular system (Moller and Philpott, 2005; Lemaire, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moller and Philpott, 2005 and Lemaire, 2011.

claim: The heart in each individual zooid in a B. schlosseri colony beats synchronously with the hearts of other zooids in the colony.
source: In contrast, the heart in each individual zooid in a B. schlosseri colony beats synchronously with the hearts of other zooids in the colony, driving a bidirectional blood flow throughout an interconnected vasculature (Video 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive observation supported by Video 1.

claim: The B. schlosseri blood system carries at least ten morphologically different cell types.
source: Moreover, this blood system carries at least ten morphologically different cell types (Schlumpberger et al., 1984; Ballarin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schlumpberger et al., 1984 and Ballarin et al., 2008.

claim: Colonial ascidians may have retained and elaborated many components of the ancestral hematopoietic program, much of which has been lost in extant solitary urochordates and cephalochordates.
source: Because of the anatomy of B. schlosseri, coupled with its hematopoietic-related gene repertoire, we hypothesize that colonial ascidians may have retained and elaborated many components of the ancestral hematopoietic program, much of which has been lost in extant solitary urochordates and cephalochordates.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their comparative genomic and anatomical observations.

claim: Among B. schlosseri homologs, there is high enrichment for gene sets predominantly expressed in human hematopoietic stem cells (14 of 20 cord blood HSC genes).
source: Among B. schlosseri homologs, we found high enrichment for gene sets predominantly expressed in human hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs; i.e., 14 of 20 cord blood HSC genes), myeloid populations (i.e., 14 of 20 early erythroid CD71+ genes), and early but not mature lymphoid populations.
evidence: This is a result from comparative gene expression analysis performed in this study.

claim: Among B. schlosseri homologs, there is high enrichment for gene sets predominantly expressed in human myeloid populations (14 of 20 early erythroid CD71+ genes).
source: Among B. schlosseri homologs, we found high enrichment for gene sets predominantly expressed in human hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs; i.e., 14 of 20 cord blood HSC genes), myeloid populations (i.e., 14 of 20 early erythroid CD71+ genes), and early but not mature lymphoid populations.
evidence: This is a result from comparative gene expression analysis performed in this study.

claim: Among B. schlosseri homologs, there is high enrichment for gene sets predominantly expressed in early but not mature human lymphoid populations.
source: Among B. schlosseri homologs, we found high enrichment for gene sets predominantly expressed in human hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs; i.e., 14 of 20 cord blood HSC genes), myeloid populations (i.e., 14 of 20 early erythroid CD71+ genes), and early but not mature lymphoid populations.
evidence: This is a result from comparative gene expression analysis performed in this study.

claim: The evolution of adaptive immunity progressed rapidly beginning with jawless vertebrates, with much of the genetic repertoire in place by the emergence of jawed vertebrates.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Bartl et al., 1994; Laird et al., 2000; Dishaw and Litman, 2009; Guo et al., 2009; Flajnik and Kasahara, 2010; Bajoghli et al., 2011; Hirano et al., 2011) this analysis indicates that the evolution of adaptive immunity progressed rapidly beginning with jawless vertebrates, with much of the genetic repertoire in place by the emergence of jawed vertebrates (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparative analysis, consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: Homologs of human genes with specific expression in HSC and blood progenitor populations appear early in metazoan evolution.
source: However, homologs of human genes with specific expression in HSC and blood progenitor populations, including T and B progenitor cells, appear early in metazoan evolution (Figure 5; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Unlike solitary tunicates (e.g., Ciona), B. schlosseri has a defined vasculature with circulating blood cells.
source: Unlike solitary tunicates (e.g., Ciona), B. schlosseri has a defined vasculature with circulating blood cells (including cells with lymphocyte-like and macrophage-like morphology; Schlumpberger et al., 1984; Ballarin et al., 2008; Video 1).
evidence: This is a comparative anatomical observation supported by citations and Video 1.

claim: B. schlosseri blood contains cells with lymphocyte-like and macrophage-like morphology.
source: Unlike solitary tunicates (e.g., Ciona), B. schlosseri has a defined vasculature with circulating blood cells (including cells with lymphocyte-like and macrophage-like morphology; Schlumpberger et al., 1984; Ballarin et al., 2008; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schlumpberger et al., 1984 and Ballarin et al., 2008.

claim: Expression of 13 HSC homologs was found in the B. schlosseri endostyle stem cell niche.
source: Strikingly, we found evidence for expression of 13 HSC homologs in the B. schlosseri endostyle stem cell niche (Voskoboynik et al., 2008), and 7 in the vasculature.
evidence: This is a result from PCR and re-sequencing experiments performed in this study.

claim: Expression of 7 HSC homologs was found in the B. schlosseri vasculature.
source: Strikingly, we found evidence for expression of 13 HSC homologs in the B. schlosseri endostyle stem cell niche (Voskoboynik et al., 2008), and 7 in the vasculature.
evidence: This is a result from PCR and re-sequencing experiments performed in this study.

claim: Expression of all 14 early erythroid CD71+ genes was confirmed in the B. schlosseri vasculature and endostyle.
source: We also confirmed expression of all 14 early erythroid CD71+ genes in the vasculature and endostyle (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a result from PCR and re-sequencing experiments performed in this study.

claim: The evolution of hematopoiesis proceeded from stem cells to myeloid populations to lymphoid populations, leading to the eventual emergence of T/B-cell based adaptive immunity in vertebrates.
source: Thus, our analysis not only identified B. schlosseri genes that may define evolutionary precursor cells of human hematopoietic lineages, but also indicates that the evolution of hematopoiesis proceeded from stem cells to myeloid populations to lymphoid populations, leading to the eventual emergence, absent in B. schlosseri, of T/B-cell based adaptive immunity in vertebrates (Figure 5; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparative analysis of hematopoietic gene expression patterns.

claim: T/B-cell based adaptive immunity is absent in B. schlosseri.
source: Thus, our analysis not only identified B. schlosseri genes that may define evolutionary precursor cells of human hematopoietic lineages, but also indicates that the evolution of hematopoiesis proceeded from stem cells to myeloid populations to lymphoid populations, leading to the eventual emergence, absent in B. schlosseri, of T/B-cell based adaptive immunity in vertebrates (Figure 5; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The B. schlosseri genome lacks significant homology to most genes known to play an important role in the vertebrate adaptive immune system.
source: Not surprisingly, the B. schlosseri genome lacks significant homology to most genes known to play an important role in the vertebrate adaptive immune system.
evidence: This is a result from the comparative genomic analysis.

claim: No evidence for assembled major histocompatibility genes could be found in the B. schlosseri genome.
source: For instance, no evidence for the following immune-related genes could be found: (i) assembled major histocompatibility genes, (ii) genes with homology to RAG1/RAG2, which are involved in immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor rearrangements, (iii) terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase, which adds nucleotides to the rearranging VDJ elements to create receptor diversity, (iv) V region subgenic elements encoding T cell and immunoglobulin antigen receptor domains, or (v) VLR like immune receptor elements found in lampreys (Weigert et al., 1970; Davis et al., 1984; Oettinger et al., 1990; Fagan and Weissman, 1998; Laird et al., 2000; Muramatsu et al., 2000; Pancer et al., 2004; Rogozin et al., 2007; Dishaw and Litman, 2009; Flajnik and Kasahara, 2010; Hirano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative genomic analysis, with citations to previous studies on these genes.

claim: No genes with homology to RAG1/RAG2 could be found in the B. schlosseri genome.
source: For instance, no evidence for the following immune-related genes could be found: (i) assembled major histocompatibility genes, (ii) genes with homology to RAG1/RAG2, which are involved in immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor rearrangements, (iii) terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase, which adds nucleotides to the rearranging VDJ elements to create receptor diversity, (iv) V region subgenic elements encoding T cell and immunoglobulin antigen receptor domains, or (v) VLR like immune receptor elements found in lampreys (Weigert et al., 1970; Davis et al., 1984; Oettinger et al., 1990; Fagan and Weissman, 1998; Laird et al., 2000; Muramatsu et al., 2000; Pancer et al., 2004; Rogozin et al., 2007; Dishaw and Litman, 2009; Flajnik and Kasahara, 2010; Hirano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative genomic analysis, with citations to previous studies on these genes.

source: For instance, no evidence for the following immune-related genes could be found: (i) assembled major histocompatibility genes, (ii) genes with homology to RAG1/RAG2, which are involved in immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor rearrangements, (iii) terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase, which adds nucleotides to the rearranging VDJ elements to create receptor diversity, (iv) V region subgenic elements encoding T cell and immunoglobulin antigen receptor domains, or (v) VLR like immune receptor elements found in lampreys (Weigert et al., 1970; Davis et al., 1984; Oettinger et al., 1990; Fagan and Weissman, 1998; Laird et al., 2000; Muramatsu et al., 2000; Pancer et al., 2004; Rogozin et al., 2007; Dishaw and Litman, 2009; Flajnik and Kasahara, 2010; Hirano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of RAG1/RAG2, supported by citations.

claim: A large fraction (approximately 45%) of intron-less genes were identified in the B. schlosseri draft genome.
source: We identified a large fraction (∼45%; Supplementary file 2H; Figure 3—figure supplement 4) of intron-less genes in the B. schlosseri draft genome, including retroviral genes such as Gag, Poli, Env and LTRs, which are used by viruses to insert their genetic sequences into the host genomes.
evidence: This is a result from the gene structure analysis, reported in Supplementary file 2H and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The B. schlosseri genome includes retroviral genes such as Gag, Poli, Env and LTRs.
source: We identified a large fraction (∼45%; Supplementary file 2H; Figure 3—figure supplement 4) of intron-less genes in the B. schlosseri draft genome, including retroviral genes such as Gag, Poli, Env and LTRs, which are used by viruses to insert their genetic sequences into the host genomes.
evidence: This is a result from the gene annotation analysis.

claim: Retroviral genes such as Gag, Poli, Env and LTRs are used by viruses to insert their genetic sequences into host genomes.
source: We identified a large fraction (∼45%; Supplementary file 2H; Figure 3—figure supplement 4) of intron-less genes in the B. schlosseri draft genome, including retroviral genes such as Gag, Poli, Env and LTRs, which are used by viruses to insert their genetic sequences into the host genomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about retroviral gene function.

claim: Adaptive immunity genes like RAG1/RAG2 are intron-less and first appear in jawed vertebrates.
source: As adaptive immunity genes like RAG1/RAG2 are intron-less and first appear in jawed vertebrates, it has been suggested that they may have originated via horizontal infections of primitive retroviral like agents, and/or gene transfer (Bartl et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Bartl et al., 1994.

claim: It has been suggested that RAG1/RAG2 may have originated via horizontal infections of primitive retroviral like agents, and/or gene transfer.
source: As adaptive immunity genes like RAG1/RAG2 are intron-less and first appear in jawed vertebrates, it has been suggested that they may have originated via horizontal infections of primitive retroviral like agents, and/or gene transfer (Bartl et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work, cited to Bartl et al., 1994.

claim: The B. schlosseri genome encodes homologues of Foxn1.
source: In addition, the B. schlosseri genome encodes homologues of Foxn1, the thymus epithelial gene mutated in the immunodeficient nude mouse (nu/nu), a marker of the thymopoietic microenvironment in vertebrates (Nehls et al., 1996; Bajoghli et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative genomic analysis, with citations to previous studies on Foxn1.

claim: Foxn1 is the thymus epithelial gene mutated in the immunodeficient nude mouse (nu/nu).
source: In addition, the B. schlosseri genome encodes homologues of Foxn1, the thymus epithelial gene mutated in the immunodeficient nude mouse (nu/nu), a marker of the thymopoietic microenvironment in vertebrates (Nehls et al., 1996; Bajoghli et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Nehls et al., 1996 and Bajoghli et al., 2011.

claim: Foxn1 is a marker of the thymopoietic microenvironment in vertebrates.
source: In addition, the B. schlosseri genome encodes homologues of Foxn1, the thymus epithelial gene mutated in the immunodeficient nude mouse (nu/nu), a marker of the thymopoietic microenvironment in vertebrates (Nehls et al., 1996; Bajoghli et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Nehls et al., 1996 and Bajoghli et al., 2011.

claim: At least some genetic circuitry relevant for vertebrate adaptive immunity was already in place in the common ancestor of the protochordate B. schlosseri and vertebrates.
source: These data indicate that at least some genetic circuitry relevant for vertebrate adaptive immunity was already in place in the common ancestor of the protochordate B. schlosseri and vertebrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The B. schlosseri mtDNA is 14,928 bp long and contains the typical complement of tunicate mt genes (24 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs and 13 proteins).
source: The mtDNA of the B. schlosseri Sc6a-b specimen is 14,928 bp long and contains the typical complement of tunicate mt genes (24 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs and 13 proteins).
evidence: This is a result from the mitochondrial genome sequencing performed in this study.

claim: The B. schlosseri genome is a community resource for studying alternative modes of reproduction, natural transplantation reactions, and stem cell-mediated regeneration.
source: The B. schlosseri genome is a community resource for studying alternative modes of reproduction, natural transplantation reactions, and stem cell-mediated regeneration.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility and significance of the genome resource.

claim: Tunicates are classified as chordates because their planktonic larva stage shares structural characteristics with all chordates: a notochord, dorsal neural tube, segmented musculature, and gill slits.
source: Tunicates are classified as chordates because their planktonic larva stage (Figure 1A) shares structural characteristics with all chordates: a notochord, dorsal neural tube, segmented musculature, and gill slits (Darwin, 1874; Dehal et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tunicate classification, supported by citations.

claim: Tunicate larvae settle in response to light and metamorphose into sessile individuals.
source: Larvae settle in response to light and metamorphose into sessile individuals (Figure 1B), which lose most of their chordate phenotypes (Darwin, 1874; Dehal et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a description of tunicate development, supported by citations.

claim: Sessile tunicate individuals lose most of their chordate phenotypes.
source: Larvae settle in response to light and metamorphose into sessile individuals (Figure 1B), which lose most of their chordate phenotypes (Darwin, 1874; Dehal et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a description of tunicate development, supported by citations.

claim: Tunicates reproduce either sexually (solitary tunicates) or sexually and asexually (colonial tunicates).
source: Tunicates reproduce either sexually (solitary tunicates; Dehal et al., 2002; Lemaire, 2011), or sexually and asexually (colonial tunicates; Manni and Burighel, 2006; Lemaire, 2011).
evidence: This is a description of tunicate reproductive strategies, supported by citations.

claim: Sexual and asexual reproduction in tunicates give rise to nearly identical complex adult body plans.
source: These two reproductive modes give rise to nearly identical complex adult body plans, including digestive and respiratory systems, a simple tube-like heart, siphons, an endostyle, a neural complex, ovary and testis (Manni and Burighel, 2006; Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is a description of tunicate anatomy, supported by citation and figures.

claim: The ability to reproduce asexually renders colonial tunicates robust survivors, capable of rapid proliferation and whole body regeneration.
source: The ability to reproduce asexually renders colonial tunicates robust survivors, capable of rapid proliferation and whole body regeneration.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the ecological advantages of asexual reproduction.

source: The sequence of the B. schlosseri mitochondrial genome has been submitted to the European Nucleotide Archive under accession number HF548551.
evidence: This is a statement about data deposition.
